This view was sup- ported by a meta-analysis.3 US guidelines for the manage- ment of sinusitis in adults4 state that most cases will re- solve without antibacterial treatment and recommend that antibacterials should be reserved for those patients with persistent moderate or severe symptoms. However, a later meta-analysis5 considered that antibacterials could not be justified, even in patients who reported symptoms for longer than 7 to 10 days; the only reason for antibacterial treatment was the presence of signs suggestive of a serious complication (such as high fever, periorbital swelling, ery- thema, or intense facial pain). Guidelines from the Ameri- can Academy of Pediatrics for the management of sinusitis in children6 recommend that antibacterials be given to children clinically diagnosed with persistent or severe acute bacterial sinusitis in order to achieve a more rapid clinical cure. If antibacterials are considered necessary, treatment should be given for an adequate length of time, usually 2 weeks.6-8 Topical decongestants may also be used to promote drain- age and ventilation.7,8 The choice of antibacterial is similar to that for acute otitis media (p.182). Effective antibacteri- als include amoxicillin with or without clavulanic acid, ce- furoxime, clarithromycin, clindamycin and azithromycin;6 the emergence of penicillin-resistant strains of H. influen- zae, M. catarrhalis, and Str. pneumoniae is of concern.9 Co-trimoxazole or erythromycin with sulfafurazole have also been used although pneumococcal resistance has been reported to be substantial.6 Patients with evidence of se- vere infections may need initial intravenous therapy with vancomycin and ceftriaxone or cefotaxime.9 Tetracycline or erythromycin are the most effective antibacterials against Chlamydophila pneumoniae.10 Failure to treat acute sinusitis that does not resolve sponta- neously can result in chronic sinusitis or occasionally in complications such as brain abscess or meningitis. Exacer- bations of chronic sinusitis are treated as for acute infec- tion. Management of chronic sinusitis is based on reducing obstruction of the sinus cavity using antihistamines, de- congestants, anti-inflammatory drugs (including cortico- steroids), and saline washes as appropriate.7,11,12 The use- fulness of antibacterials is more contentious,11 although some clinicians advocate prolonged courses as part of ini- tial treatment.7,12 As well as their established antibacterial effect, it has been suggested that macrolides also have im- munomodulatory effects that could be useful in the man- agement of respiratory diseases including chronic sinusitis but large placebo-controlled studies are needed. Surgical intervention may be necessary if medical treatment fails.
